editorNote: The home-computer price war has claimed another famous name, even as ambitious graphics machines and a crowded software trade show point toward what comes next.
morningLine: Timex leaves the Sinclair computer business while Softcon fills New Orleans with software, graphics and argument.

lead.headline: Timex Pulls the Plug on Its Sinclair Home Computers
lead.dek: The watchmaker joins Texas Instruments and Mattel in retreat, turning the post-boom home-computer shakeout into the week’s unmistakable story.
body: Timex will cease production and sales of its Timex/Sinclair 1500 and 2068 home computers, ending one of the most visible attempts to put a microcomputer into American homes at a mass-market price. The company says manufacturing will stop after remaining components are used, probably within four months.

Only a short time ago, the sub-$100 Timex/Sinclair 1000 commanded an estimated 28 percent of the home market. But aggressive competition from Commodore and Texas Instruments forced reductions on the later 1500 and 2068, while the collapse of the 1983 price war left retailers and manufacturers with painful inventories.

Timex marketing vice president C. Michael Jacobi calls the market “risky and volatile.” The withdrawal puts Timex beside Texas Instruments and Mattel among major consumer names backing away from home computers, and it raises a sober question for buyers: which inexpensive machine will still have software and service next year?

Sinclair insists its own business and planned $500 direct-mail launch of the 32-bit QL will continue. Timex’s Dundee plant is also expected to remain Sinclair’s largest contract manufacturer. The brand partnership may persist behind factory doors, but on American store shelves the Timex/Sinclair experiment is ending.

stories.headline: Mindset Bets Its PC Future on Spectacular Graphics
body: Former Atari computer chief Roger Badertscher is preparing an April launch for Mindset, a $1,099 80186-based machine built around custom graphics coprocessors. Its animation and color modes aim at a creative market that ordinary IBM compatibles barely address.

Storage sharply raises the bill: one floppy adds $699 and two drives add $1,299. Mindset says it tested 60 unmodified IBM PC programs, plans Microsoft Windows support and will offer the $399 Lumena graphics package. A $40 joystick makes the system’s game and animation ambitions plain.

stories.headline: VisiCalc Partners Carry Their Feud to Softcon
body: Software Arts, creator of VisiCalc, has announced its own Advanced Version for IBM PCs after moving to end its long marketing arrangement with VisiCorp. A Massachusetts court refused VisiCorp’s request to stop Software Arts from using the famous trademark.

Owners can obtain a promotional $99.95 upgrade, but the six months of suits and countersuits expose a new software-industry reality: a program name, its distribution rights and its installed audience can be as valuable as the code itself.

stories.headline: Model 100 Gains a Desktop-Sized Disk Drive
body: Radio Shack’s portable Model 100 can now connect to a $799, 5.25-inch disk unit, with room for a $240 second drive. Each single-sided floppy holds 184K in a format incompatible with other TRS-80 disks.

The enclosure is not portable, but it adds monitor and television connections and a 25-line display. For owners of a 16K or larger Model 100, the accessory turns a road machine into a more capable office system when it returns to the desk.

undergroundDesk.headline: Louisiana Moves Against Software Piracy
undergroundDesk.dek: A proposed state law would turn shrink-wrap licenses into a new legal weapon.
body: Louisiana officials used Softcon to announce legislation aimed at unauthorized software duplication and distribution. The proposal would treat opening or buying a package as acceptance of the license enclosed inside.

Copy-protection vendor Vault Corporation, maker of Prolok, helped draft much of the bill. Its advocates call the measure a balance between publishers and customers; if enacted, Louisiana would become the first state with such a law.
